name: Felix Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the housing benefit team at the city benefits office on Market Street, five years now. Most mornings I clear the overnight claims queue, chase landlords for tenancy agreements and ring people whose rent payments got stopped by mistake. The part I like is when I get someone's payment back on before the eviction letter lands. What wears me out is the system itself, three screens that don't talk to each other and a manager counting how many cases I close an hour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with most closely, and how do you feel about the tools you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sit next to Gloria, who's been there twenty years and knows every rule by heart. I'm also the union rep for our floor, so people bring me their gripes over lunch. I don't use any of the AI stuff, not even the chat assistant they put on our desktops last spring. I'd rather read the file myself, because the file is a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, honestly, in the union group chat. Management spent a fortune on that desktop assistant and it mostly writes letters nobody reads. I'd post something like: the work was always people, not paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but I'd still be fed up. The office is still short-staffed, my caseload is still around 140, and the hourly targets don't go away just because the robots flopped. My job's safe, it just isn't getting any easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it and keep pushing the union on caseload limits. I'd put another few hundred a month into savings, because Lena (my partner) and I want a deposit on a flat in about three years. I wouldn't touch the AI assistant even if they made it better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the job, but tired. The pressure on the team is still there, it's just the old kind of pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing much changes. What would still be hard for you at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The targets. Our manager, Dariusz, gets told from above that the assistant saves eight minutes a case, so they cut our time to match, even though it doesn't. If AI turns out to be hype, I'd be fighting for those eight minutes back for the next two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lena see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena (my partner) is a nurse, so she'd laugh and say her ward never believed in it. She'd also say I spend too many evenings on union stuff. She's probably right.

say: I'd tell the union chat the **desktop assistant** was money wasted that should have paid for staff.
I'd say the job was always about **people**, not paperwork, and this proves it.
think: My **job is safe**, but the caseload of about 140 and the hourly targets stay heavy.
The real fight is getting back the **eight minutes** per case that management cut for the assistant.
do: Keep working cases by hand and push the union for **caseload limits** this year.
Save a few hundred more a month toward a **flat deposit** with Lena in three years.
feel: **Calm** about keeping the job, but **tired** of the same old staffing pressure.
S0.quote: My job's safe, it just isn't getting any easier.
fieldNote: Felix sounds relieved at first, but the **staffing** grievance runs through everything.
He frames AI mainly as a **management excuse** to cut time per case.
Even with no big change, the hourly **targets** keep him uneasy rather than calm.

steps.text: Work each housing benefit case by hand without the desktop assistant
Raise caseload limits at the next union branch meeting
Put an extra 300 a month toward a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is exactly why we need the union at the table before anything gets switched on. Online I'd probably write something angry about ministers swapping caseworkers for software that can't hear someone crying on the phone. I'd say it loudly, because if nobody says it they'll just do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my desk is the first one they'd automate. Housing benefit is mostly checking documents, writing letters and answering the same five questions, and that's exactly what the card lists. I think the team of twelve becomes six within three years, and I'm not the person who's going to learn the new system fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard on the union side first, getting a no-redundancy agreement before the rollout. I'd also start looking quietly at jobs where you sit with people, like tenancy support at a housing charity, maybe the one on Dock Road where my friend Amira works. I'd keep the savings untouched, because that's my safety net if it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my stomach turn a bit. I chose this job because it felt steady and useful, and now it would feel like I'm waiting in a queue to be replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gloria, without a doubt. She's 58, she's brilliant with the rules, and she'd be lost with a new screen that does the rules for her. I'd be worried for myself too, but I'm 27 and I've got savings, so I can't pretend it's the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use the AI tools. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I know that's stubborn. If they forced it on me I'd use it the minimum. I'd rather move to a job where the human part is the whole job than be the person who clicks approve on what the machine decided.

say: I'd tell colleagues the **union** must be at the table before any system is switched on.
I'd post that **ministers** are swapping caseworkers for software that can't hear people in distress.
think: My desk is mostly **checking and letters**, so it's the first thing they'd automate.
I expect the **team of twelve** to halve within three years, and I won't adapt fastest.
do: Push for a **no-redundancy deal** before the new system rolls out next year.
Apply quietly for **tenancy support** jobs at the housing charity on Dock Road.
Leave the **savings** untouched as a safety net in case I'm cut.
feel: **Sick** at the idea of waiting in line to be replaced.
**Guilty** that colleagues like Gloria have far less room to move than he does.
S1.quote: I'd rather move to a job where the human part is the whole job than be the person who clicks approve on what the machine decided.
fieldNote: He sees his own role as **high exposure** and says so plainly.
His answer to change is **organising**, not learning the new tools.
Worry for older colleague **Gloria** shapes his sense of fairness.
He is already eyeing a **people-facing** exit at a charity.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a no-redundancy agreement before rollout
Apply for tenancy support roles at the Dock Road housing charity
Leave the savings untouched as a fallback fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster that nobody voted for, and I'd say it everywhere. I'd be at every union meeting and probably on the march outside the ministry. I'd tell people the government has a duty to everyone it just made jobless, starting with its own staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone by 2028, full stop. Everything I do is thinking work at a screen, so I get no extra time at all. The only part a machine can't do yet is sit in a flat with someone whose ceiling is leaking, and the robots come three years later for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Lena and do the sums: about nine months of savings, her nursing job, and the flat plans paused. I'd join the campaign for an income guarantee and push the union to fight for retraining money. Then I'd look at hands-on care or support work, because that gives me roughly until 2031 before robots catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Two years is nothing. I'd be lying awake doing the maths on the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not buying the flat, not yet. I'd tell her I'm sorry I was the one saying public sector jobs were safe. She'd probably be calmer than me, because nurses are hands-on and she'd have those three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care work. Would you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, though I'd hate how it happened. I've visited enough people at home to know I can do it. Moving into care work feels like being pushed off a cliff onto a ledge that's only there for three more years.

say: I'd call it a **disaster** nobody voted for and join the march outside the ministry.
I'd say the government owes its **own staff** first, and everyone else it made jobless.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**, because nearly all of it is screen work.
Hands-on support work only buys about **three years** before robots arrive too.
do: Sit down with Lena in the first month and **pause** the flat purchase.
Campaign through the union for an **income guarantee** and retraining money.
Apply for hands-on **care or support work** to last until robots arrive.
feel: **Scared** and awake at night doing the household sums.
**Ashamed** of having told people public sector jobs were safe.
S2.quote: Moving into care work feels like being pushed off a cliff onto a ledge that's only there for three more years.
fieldNote: Felix expects **certain job loss** and links it directly to his screen-based work.
He understands the **three-year gap** and sees it as a short ledge, not a refuge.
Lena's **nursing job** is the household's anchor in this picture.
His resistance to tech pushes him toward **care work** rather than AI work.

steps.text: Pause the flat deposit plan with Lena in the first month
Campaign through the union for an income guarantee
Apply for hands-on care or support jobs before 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like with the fast one, I'd say the union has to move now, but at least there'd be time to win something. I'd tell people at work that five years is enough to demand a proper transition fund. Online I'd keep pushing for rules on what government can hand to machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same end for my job, just with a countdown I can see. My work is all thinking work, so 2031 is my date. I'd have a few years to get into something hands-on, which buys me until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening course in social care, maybe a certificate in supported housing work. I'd keep saving, about a third of my pay, so Lena and I have a bigger cushion. I'd stay in the benefits office until it actually starts shrinking, because the pay is good and I'm not leaving early for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panicky than the fast one, but a slow dread. It's like knowing the date your contract ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me plan the jump into care work instead of just falling. With two years I'd grab any job. With five I'd retrain properly and still keep the flat dream alive, maybe smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still blame the same people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the ministers who'd sign the contracts. Five years is time to put rules in place, so if they don't, that's on them.

say: I'd tell work the union must **act now** while there's time to win something.
I'd push online for **rules** on what government can hand over to machines.
think: My job still **ends in 2031**, because it's all thinking work.
Moving into hands-on work buys me until about **2034**, which is something.
do: Start an **evening course** in supported housing work within the first year.
Save about **a third** of my pay to build a bigger cushion.
Stay at the benefits office until **cuts actually start**, then move.
feel: A **slow dread**, like knowing the date a contract ends.
S3.quote: Five years would let me plan the jump into care work instead of just falling.
fieldNote: The extra time turns his fear into a **plan**, but not into comfort.
He still places the **blame** squarely on ministers.
He keeps the **well-paid** job as long as possible before moving.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening certificate in supported housing work
Save about a third of each month's pay
Lobby through the union for a public transition fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this decently, so there's no excuse if they don't. At work I'd push for a deal where every caseworker gets paid retraining. Online I'd be the boring guy posting about transition funds again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'm 37 when the thinking work goes, and that's young enough to start over. That's a strange comfort. I'd probably still be in this job for five or six of those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep saving, and Lena and I would probably buy the flat after all, a small one. Around year three or four I'd train in something hands-on, maybe as a support worker or even an occupational therapy assistant. I'd keep up the union work the whole way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like heavy weather than a storm. I'd have time to think straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good outcome look like for you in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be doing support work with real people, in a job I chose, not one I fell into. The flat would be paid down a bit. Gloria would have retired on her own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy the flat. Is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, a bit. But Lena's job is hands-on and I'd have years of savings, so I think we'd manage. I'd rather not let a ten-year forecast stop us living.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time**, so there's no excuse for a bad transition.
I'd push for a deal giving every caseworker **paid retraining**.
think: I'll be **37** when the thinking work goes, young enough to start over.
I'd probably stay in this job for **five or six** more years.
do: Buy a **small flat** with Lena and keep saving alongside the mortgage.
Train as a **support worker** or therapy assistant around year three or four.
Keep up the **union work** for a fair transition the whole way.
feel: **Uneasy**, like heavy weather rather than a storm, with time to think.
S4.quote: Ten years means I'm 37 when the thinking work goes, and that's young enough to start over.
fieldNote: The long runway lets him keep **life plans** like the flat going.
He still expects his current job to **end**, so he stays anxious.
Hope rests on choosing **people-facing work** rather than falling into it.

steps.text: Buy a small flat with Lena while both still earn
Train as a support worker or therapy assistant around 2030
Keep pushing the union for paid retraining for caseworkers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because two years isn't enough for anyone, least of all a government office. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, and the union having a real say in how the systems get switched on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who picks up when the system fails. Right now the person who answers the phone when the machine gets it wrong is me, and in every one of these pictures I'm not sure it's anyone.

headlineQuote: Right now the person who answers the phone when the machine gets it wrong is me, and in every one of these pictures I'm not sure it's anyone.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old** housing benefit caseworker and floor union rep who never uses AI tools.
He knows his job is **screen work** and expects it to shrink fast under real disruption.
His response is **union organising** and a move toward hands-on support or care work.
His partner Lena's **nursing job** and nine months of savings steady the household.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years gives nobody, least of all government, time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** during retraining and a real union say over how systems are switched on.
